title: Lester Melrose, Ham Fatsher blues and the double recording
summary: Melrose asked for something like Papa Charlie Jackson; Burton composed his blues, recorded for Gennett, then Melrose had him record the same number for Paramount.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: So I kept on fooling around, doing those novelty numbers with washboard, playing the horn, singing and jiving, that kind of stuff until years passed in between. And Lester Melrose come along. We know him too, because he used to deal with Jell-O'-Morton during the time when I was fooling around with Jell-O, way back in the early 20s. So me and Mr. Melrose got together and got to talking. And so I said, Mr. Melrose, I said, I've got a lot of good stuff I know that could sell. He said, well what is it buddy? I said, well I want to record by myself to sing and play the piano. I said, all this is, I had a lot of recording with bands and all of their numbers. I said, but I want to do a number by myself on the piano and sing. And he said, well, what is it? You know how short they're all in the waxes? You come up with the same thing Dean Quilliams come up with now. I said, but I tell you what I do. I says, I got a couple of blues. I got some little ballad numbers and some of them semi-classic with nice words to it. And he said, well, okay then, I'll listen to them. And he come out south side there at 45th Michigan, at Jimmy Blight's house, listen to me playing and singing these things. And so at that time Papa Charlie Jackson was going big with the, he's playing the guitar and singing Uncle Bud and all them type of blues. And so Melrose had a lot of confidence in me with the different variety of numbers I was composing. He says, but he says, can't you get something together, something like Papa Charlie Jackson, and his blues is going so big? And I said, well, yeah. I said, I think I can come up with something like that. So we had a kind of a holiday after Christmas holidays was over. And we musicians got together and had a little celebration. And so they know I liked eggnog and never did too much drinking. So I got to drinking a couple of glasses of eggnog and singing and clown with the rest of them. And I come up with those blues. I call them Ham Fatsher blues. Do you remember what it was?

And so after the house went down with them, so I said, well, I'll take business with pleasure. I think I'll call Mr. Melrose up tomorrow and tell him I've got just what he wants. Yeah. And that's what I did. I called him up the next day and told him, I said, Mr. Melrose, I think I've got the thing that you want, something like Papa Charlie Jackson's putting out. He said, yeah, what is it? So and so. I said, well, he said, if you show that you've got it, I'll set for the recording tomorrow morning, a special recording. He said, and you meet me at Lion Healings building. And I met him at Lion Healings building. That's when he set me up for this recording and I recorded for the Jeanette people. But the big mistake was that Melrose was, he was trying to make all the money and put out the situation. And so he called me up the very next day and had me recorded for the Paramount people.
The same number. Oh, yeah. I noticed some of those numbers there are the same thing. That's what that's what they're saying.
